---
title: Spotting the weird ones
author: Rob J Hyndman
date: 1 December 2026
url: robjhyndman.com/wombat2026
abstract: >-
  Data analysis is about finding the stories hidden in the mass of information that make up a data set.
  Usually we are interested in understanding the major patterns — the relationships that hold true for most of the data.
  But sometimes we need to look at the weird observations, the mavericks, the ones that don't follow the crowd and behave differently.
  These observations are called "anomalies".
  Many anomaly detection methods have been developed, but they are often based on ad hoc rules and hidden assumptions, and can lead to misleading conclusions.
  Instead, I will describe a principled statistical approach to identifying anomalies in diverse data sets, from simple numerical data to complex high-dimensional data objects.
  The ideas will be illustrated using the weird package for R applied to several data analysis problems, including spotting over-priced wines, identifying errors in the records of the Old Faithful Geyser, and uncovering forgotten epidemics in 19th century France.
format:
  presentation-revealjs+letterbox:

## Spot the anomaly {.nostretch}

```{r}
#| label: fig_spot
#| results: asis

# Each plot, then a hand-drawn circle (roughnotation extension) round its
# anomaly: fragment indices 1 and 3, with plot b appearing at 2. The circle is
# drawn round an empty span placed over the anomaly in percentages of the plot.
files <- tar_read(fig_spot_pngs)
boxes <- tar_read(spot_boxes)
spot_plot <- function(file, box, left, index, circle_index) {
  cat(
    "\n::: {.absolute .spot-fig top=\"95\" left=\"",
    left,
    "\" width=\"520\"",
    if (index > 0) paste0(" .fragment fragment-index=\"", index, "\""),
    "}\n![](",
    file,
    ")\n\n",
    "[]{.rn-fragment fragment-index=\"",
    circle_index,
    "\" rn-type=\"circle\"",
    " rn-color=\"#c14b14\" rn-strokewidth=\"3\" rn-padding=\"0\"",
    sprintf(
      " style=\"left: %.3f%%; top: %.3f%%; width: %.3f%%; height: %.3f%%\"}\n:::\n",
      100 * box[["left"]],
      100 * box[["top"]],
      100 * box[["width"]],
      100 * box[["width"]]
    ),
    sep = ""
  )
}
spot_plot(files[1], boxes$a, 40, 0, 1)
spot_plot(files[2], boxes$b, 720, 2, 3)
```

::: {.absolute .fragment top="630" left="0" width="1280" fragment-index="4"}
::::: {.alertblock}
An anomaly is an observation in a region of **low probability density**.
:::::
:::

## Surprisal probabilities {.nostretch}

::: {.alertblock}
The probability of an observation at least as unlikely as $y_i$ under density $f$:

$$
  p_i = \mathbb{P}\big(f(Y) \le f(y_i)\big), \qquad Y \sim f
$$
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig_sp
#| results: asis

files <- tar_read(fig_sp_png)
cat("\n::: {.r-stack .sp-stack}\n")
for (step in seq_along(files)) {
  cat(if (step == 1) "\n::: {.step}\n" else "\n::: {.fragment}\n")
  cat("![](", files[step], "){width=1800}\n", sep = "")
  cat("\n:::\n")
}
cat("\n:::\n")
```

::: {.absolute .fragment top="300" left="740" width="480"}
::::: {.alertblock}
An observation is an **anomaly with respect to $f$** if $p_i < \alpha$.
:::::
:::

## Surprisal probabilities in R

![](images/weird-hex.png){.absolute top="0" right="0" width="190"}

::: {.larger}
::::: {style="width: 82%"}
<code>surprisals_prob(<span class="fragment arg-hl arg-object" data-fragment-index="1">object</span>, <span class="fragment arg-hl arg-distribution" data-fragment-index="2">distribution</span>, \.\.\.)</code> returns a surprisal probability for each observation in `object` under model `distribution`.
:::::

::::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
- [`object`]{.arg-object}: a vector, matrix, data frame or factor, or a fitted `lm`, `glm` or `gam` (which supplies data and distribution).
:::::

::::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"}
- [`distribution`]{.arg-distribution}: any **distributional** object; a kernel density estimate by default for numerical data.
:::::
:::

## Surprisal probabilities in R

::: {.code-steps data-steps="2:1,3:2,4:3"}
<!-- panache-ignore-format-start -->
```{r}
#| label: normal-eg
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

N01 <- dist_normal(mean = 0, sd = 1)
tibble(y = generate(N01, times = 1000)[[1]]) |>
  mutate(p = surprisals_prob(y, distribution = N01)) |>
  arrange(p)
```
<!-- panache-ignore-format-end -->
:::

## Approximate extreme surprisal probabilities {#part-approximate-extreme-surprisal-probabilities .section-slide background-color="#0f2a44"}

`r section("Approximate extreme surprisal probabilities")`

## Surprisals

::: {.alertblock}
The **surprisal** of an observation $y_i$ under density $f$ is $s_i = -\log f(y_i)$.
:::

Surprisals are already familiar:

::: {.cards}
::::: {.block}
[Machine learning]{.block-title}

Log loss (cross-entropy)
:::::

::::: {.block}
[Information theory]{.block-title}

Expected surprisal = entropy
:::::

::::: {.block}
[Statistics]{.block-title}

Sum of surprisals = [$-$log likelihood]{style="white-space: nowrap"}
:::::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Small density $\Leftrightarrow$ large surprisal $\Leftrightarrow$ small surprisal probability.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::::: {.alertblock}
Anomalies are extreme values of the surprisals.
:::::
:::

## Surprisal probabilities

::: {.alertblock}
$$
  p_i = \mathbb{P}\big(f(Y) \le f(y_i)\big)
      = \mathbb{P}\big(-\log f(Y) \ge s_i\big), \qquad Y \sim f
$$
:::

::: {.incremental}
- $y_i$ can be multivariate, functional, an image, …
- $f$ can be assumed, estimated, conditional, …
- If $f$ is wrong, $p_i$ is wrong.
- But we can use [extreme value theory]{.alert}: the upper tail of the surprisal distribution is approximately a Generalised Pareto Distribution (GPD), even if $f$ is wrong.
- So $p_i \approx$ tail probability of a GPD fitted to the largest surprisals.
:::

## Approximate GPD surprisal probabilities

```{r}
#| label: fig_gpd
#| results: asis

files <- tar_read(fig_gpd_files)
cat_png_stack(files[1:4], video = files[5:6], video_after = 2)
```

::: {.fragment}
::::: {.alertblock}
Only needs $f$ to get the *ordering* of the extreme surprisals correct.
:::::
:::

## Hampel identifier {.nostretch}

````{r}
#| label: fig_hampel
#| results: asis

# Stages: series; first window; window tracing the median (video);
# difference; Normal. Fragment indices match the equations and bullets below.
files <- tar_read(fig_hampel_png)
video <- htmltools::tagAppendAttributes(
  video_tag(tar_read(hampel_video)),
  style = "width:100%"
)
cat("\n::: {.r-stack}\n\n")
cat("![](", files[1], "){width=100%}\n\n", sep = "")
cat("::: {.fragment fragment-index=\"1\"}\n")
cat("![](", files[2], "){width=100%}\n:::\n\n", sep = "")
cat(
  "::: {.fragment fragment-index=\"2\"}\n```{=html}\n",
  as.character(video),
  "\n```\n:::\n\n",
  sep = ""
)
for (i in 3:4) {
  cat("::: {.fragment fragment-index=\"", i + 1, "\"}\n", sep = "")
  cat("![](", files[i], "){width=100%}\n:::\n\n", sep = "")
}
cat(":::\n")
````

::: {.columns}
::::: {.column .math-left width="52%"}
::::::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
$$
  m_t = \text{median}(y_{t-w}, \dots, y_{t+w})
$$
:::::::

::::::: {.fragment fragment-index="3"}
$$
  a_t = \text{median}(|y_{t-w} - m_t|, \dots, |y_{t+w} - m_t|)
$$
:::::::

::::::: {.fragment fragment-index="4"}
- Anomaly if $|y_t - m_t| > ka_t$
:::::::
:::::
::::: {.column width="48%"}
::::::: {.fragment fragment-index="5"}
- Implicit model: $y_t \sim \text{N}(m_t, \sigma_t^2)$ with $\sigma_t = a_t/0.6745$
:::::::
::::::: {.fragment fragment-index="6"}
- Better: compute surprisals under Normal, with probabilities from GPD
:::::::
:::::
:::

## Anomaly detection using forecast distributions

```{r}
#| label: fig_pbs_roll
#| results: asis

files <- tar_read(fig_pbs_roll_files)
cat_png_stack(files[1:4], video = files[5:6])
```

::: {.fragment}
ETS refitted monthly for every series.
Points: [$p < 0.01$]{style="color: #F39B00"}, [$p < 0.001$]{style="color: #c14b14"}.
:::

::: {.notes}
ETS is refitted each month, so a level shift is flagged when it happens and then becomes the "new normal".
ETS forecast distributions are Gaussian, so $p_{i,t+1}$ is a two-sided $z$-test on the one-step forecast error.
:::

## A first iteration: $t = 36$ (first 3 years, to June 1994)

::: {.code-steps data-steps="2:1,3-5:2,6:3,7:4"}
<!-- panache-ignore-format-start -->
```{r}
#| label: pbsfc
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

pbs_fc <- pbs |>
  filter(t <= 36) |>
  group_by_key() |>
  filter(cumsum(Scripts) > 0, n() >= 36) |>
  ungroup() |>
  model(ets = ETS(Scripts)) |>
  forecast(h = 1)
```
<!-- panache-ignore-format-end -->
:::

```{r}
#| label: pbsfc_print
#| results: asis

cat_output_steps(tar_read(pbs_fc_steps), n = 4, width = Inf)
```

## A first iteration: $t = 36$ (first 3 years, to June 1994)

::: {.code-steps data-steps="2:1,3:2,4:3"}
<!-- panache-ignore-format-start -->
```{r}
#| label: pbsfc_compare
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

pbs_fc |>
  rename(fcast = Scripts) |>
  left_join(pbs, by = c("ATC2", "Month")) |>
  mutate(prob = surprisals_prob(Scripts, distribution = fcast))
```

## Surprisal probabilities as p-values

- If the forecast distribution is right, $p_{i,t} \sim \text{U}(0,1)$

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
- Flag $p_{i,t} < \alpha$: false alarms at rate $\alpha$ per series per month
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig_pbs_pvalues
#| results: asis

cat_png_stack(
  c(tar_read(fig_pbs_pvalues1_png), tar_read(fig_pbs_pvalues2_png)),
  indices = 1
)
```

::: {.notes}
Months with no scripts are left out of the histogram: when a series drops to zero, ETS forecasts zero with a tiny variance, so the surprisal distribution is not continuous and observed zeros get $p$ close to 1.
Most of the excess near zero comes from months when many series are unusual at once (see the slides on anomalies across several series); the rest is because the Gaussian forecast distributions have tails that are too thin.
:::

## Forecast distribution anomalies

```{r}
#| label: fig_pbs_anomalies

include_png(tar_read(fig_pbs_anomalies_png))
```

## Anomalies across several series

Some months are unusual in many series at once.

- $N_t$ of the $M_t$ series have $p_{i,t} < 0.001$
- Independent series: $N_t \sim \text{Binomial}(M_t, \pi)$
- Surprisal probability: $\mathbb{P}(N_t \ge n_t)$
- $\pi$ estimated from all previous months

::: {.notes}
If the forecast densities were correct, $\pi$ would be 0.001.
ETS forecast densities are too narrow, so the actual rate is much higher: the orange part of the first bar in the histogram.
:::

## One idea, many kinds of data

| Data             | Density $f$                                 |
| :--------------- | :------------------------------------------ |
| Wine prices      | Normal regression model for log price       |
| Old Faithful     | Kernel density estimate (leave-one-out)     |
| French mortality | Normal centred on a moving median           |
| PBS scripts      | One-step forecast density from an ETS model |

::: {.fragment}
::::: {.alertblock}
- Surprisal probabilities: $p_i = \mathbb{P}\big(f(Y) \le f(y_i)\big)$
- GPD tail keeps $p_i$ approximately right even when $f$ is wrong
:::::

```{=html}
<script>
// Play a video when the fragment containing it is shown; rewind it when hidden
window.addEventListener("load", function () {
  function videos(e) {
    return e.fragments.flatMap(function (f) {
      return Array.from(f.querySelectorAll("video"));
    });
  }
  Reveal.on("fragmentshown", function (e) {
    videos(e).forEach(function (v) {
      v.currentTime = 0;
      v.play();
    });
  });
  Reveal.on("fragmenthidden", function (e) {
    videos(e).forEach(function (v) {
      v.pause();
      v.currentTime = 0;
    });
  });
});
</script>
```

```{=html}
<script>
// Reveal code lines in steps: data-steps="4-6:3,7:4" makes lines 4-6 a
// fragment with index 3 and line 7 a fragment with index 4. A pipe ending
// the line before each step appears with that step, so the last visible line
// never ends in a dangling pipe. Runs before Reveal is initialised, so the new
// fragments are picked up.
document.querySelectorAll(".code-steps[data-steps]").forEach(function (div) {
  var lines = div.querySelectorAll("pre code > span[id]");
  div.dataset.steps.split(",").forEach(function (step) {
    var parts = step.split(":");
    var range = parts[0].split("-").map(Number);
    for (var i = range[0]; i <= (range[1] || range[0]); i++) {
      lines[i - 1].classList.add("fragment");
      lines[i - 1].dataset.fragmentIndex = parts[1];
    }
    var prev = lines[range[0] - 2];
    var pipe = prev && Array.from(prev.querySelectorAll("span.sc")).pop();
    if (pipe && pipe.textContent === "|>" && prev.textContent.trimEnd().endsWith("|>")) {
      pipe.classList.add("fragment");
      pipe.dataset.fragmentIndex = parts[1];
    }
  });
});
</script>
```
